abstract: First post in EPI's Class of 2026 series (May 7, 2026). Young college graduates (ages 22–27 with only a bachelor's degree) saw unemployment rise from a low of 4.0% in July 2023 to 5.3% in March 2026, faster than the overall rate (3.6% to 4.3%); young noncollege workers rose 1.2 points to 7.1% since March 2024. EPI finds that nearly all (98%) of the 2024–2026 rise in young-graduate unemployment came from higher labor force participation, with their employment-to-population ratio steady since 2024, and argues it is premature to read the rise as AI substituting for entry-level white-collar work. Real median wages of young graduates rose 0.4% over the past year and 7.4% since 2019. The college wage premium peaked around 2015 and stands at 55.2% overall.
keyFindings: Young-graduate unemployment rose from 4.0% (July 2023) to 5.3% (March 2026); overall rate rose from 3.6% to 4.3%.
98% of the 2024–2026 increase in young-graduate unemployment was driven by labor force growth; EPOP held steady.
Young noncollege unemployment rose 1.2 points to 7.1% since March 2024.
Real median wages of young graduates +0.4% since 2025 and +7.4% since 2019.
College wage premium 55.2%, roughly late-1990s levels, after peaking around 2015.
methodology: EPI analysis of CPS basic monthly microdata (EPI extracts v2026.4.13); 12-month moving averages, latest April 2025–March 2026; young college graduates defined as ages 22–27 with only a four-year degree, enrolled students included.
qualifiers: Tier 3: think-tank blog post (ingest.md places think-tank blogs at Tier 3); descriptive CPS analysis with no exposure-based design. EPI's inference against an AI explanation rests on comparisons across education groups, not a causal test.
